title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
hints: if you sort jobs by end time, then for any job you decide to take, all jobs compatible with it (that ended by the time it starts) come from a contiguous prefix of that sorted order

define dp[i] as the max profit achievable using only the first i jobs (in end-time sorted order); dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], profit[i-1] + dp[j]) where j is the count of jobs that end at or before job i-1's start time

finding j - the number of earlier jobs compatible with the current one - is a search for the rightmost end time <= this job's start time, which is exactly what binary search over the sorted end times gives you in O(log n)
dp[i-1] represents 'skip job i-1', and profit[i-1] + dp[j] represents 'take job i-1 and combine with the best compatible earlier subset' - the answer is dp[n]
keep the end times of the sorted jobs in a separate array so you can binary search over them directly
commonMistakes: sorting by start time instead of end time, which breaks the 'compatible jobs form a prefix' property the DP relies on
using a strict less-than instead of less-than-or-equal in the binary search, which would wrongly forbid a job that starts exactly when another ends
forgetting the dp[i-1] (skip this job) branch and only ever taking jobs, which misses cases where skipping a low-profit job leads to a better combination later
recomputing the best compatible subset with a linear scan instead of binary search, degrading to O(n^2) when O(n log n) is achievable
off-by-one between the job index and the dp array index after sorting

content.problemStatement:
You're given n jobs, where job `i` starts at `startTime[i]`, ends at
`endTime[i]`, and pays `profit[i]`. You can only work on one job at a
time, but if a job ends at time X, you may immediately start a different
job that begins at time X.

**Return the maximum total profit obtainable by choosing a subset of non-overlapping jobs.**

Ending and starting at the same instant is not a conflict.
notes: a single job (answer is just its profit)
every job mutually overlaps, so at most one can ever be picked
every job is already non-overlapping, so the answer is the sum of all profits
a job ends exactly when another begins, which is allowed and not a conflict

sampleTestCases.explanation: take the job from 1 to 3 (profit 50) and the job from 3 to 6 (profit 70)
take the jobs from 1 to 3 (profit 20), 4 to 6 (profit 70), and 6 to 9 (profit 60): 20 + 70 + 60 = 150, which beats taking the single 3 to 10 job worth 100
all three jobs overlap with each other at time 1, so you can only take one; the best single job pays 6

optimal.time: O(n log n) for sorting and the binary searches
optimal.pattern: sort jobs by end time, then dynamic programming where dp[i] is the best profit using only the first i jobs (in sorted order), with binary search to find the last job compatible with job i

bruteForce.approach: sort jobs by start time and recursively try, for each job, either skipping it or taking it (jumping ahead to the first job whose start time is >= this job's end time); take the max over both choices, optionally memoized by job index
bruteForce.time: O(2^n) without memoization, O(n^2) with memoization (n choices for the next non-overlapping job)
bruteForce.space: O(n) recursion depth, O(n^2) with memoization
